title: Teaching, the Sangha and the Last Journey
bigQuestion: How do Buddhist texts describe the Buddha's forty-five years of teaching and his last days?

story.title: The Mustard Seed
story.kicker: A mother carrying her sick child goes door to door looking for a mustard seed.
paragraphs: Buddhist commentaries tell this story. A young mother named Kisa Gotami had one little son. He grew sick and died. Kisa Gotami could not accept it. She carried him from house to house, asking for medicine.
People shook their heads. Some thought her grief had made her lose her way. At last, someone kindly told her, "Go to the Buddha. He may be able to help you."
She found the Buddha and asked him for medicine. The story says he answered gently. "Bring me a mustard seed from a house where no one has ever died." Mustard seeds were common. Every house had some.
She went from door to door. Each family wanted to help. But every family said, "We have lost someone too." A grandmother. A father. A child. By evening, she had no seed.
Kisa Gotami sat down, still holding her son. The story says she understood that loss comes to every family. She laid her son to rest. Then she returned to the Buddha and, the texts say, became a nun.
story.think: Why do you think the Buddha asked for a mustard seed instead of just explaining?

lessons.title: In the Deer Park
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists say the Buddha gave his first sermon to five companions in the Deer Park at Sarnath.
reading: After his awakening, the Buddha wondered if anyone could understand what he had found. The texts say he decided to teach. He walked to a Deer Park near Varanasi, a place now called *Sarnath*.
There he met the five ascetics who had left him. They agreed to listen. The Buddha taught them the middle way and the Four Noble Truths. This talk is Samyutta Nikaya 56.11.
Buddhists call it "Setting the Wheel of the Dharma in Motion." The texts say one listener, Kondanna, understood right away. He became the first follower to see the truth for himself.

words.d: the Deer Park near Varanasi where the Buddha gave his first sermon

look.title: The Wheel and the Deer
look.text: Many temples show a golden wheel with eight spokes. Two deer kneel on either side, looking up at it. The wheel stands for the teaching. The deer stand for the Deer Park.
look.prompt: Why might Buddhists use a wheel as a picture for teaching?

check.q: Where was the first sermon?
check.why: Buddhists say the first sermon was in the Deer Park at Sarnath.

check.q: Who heard the first sermon?
check.why: The Buddha taught the five companions who had left him.

check.q: Who understood first, say the texts?
check.why: The texts say Kondanna understood right away.

lessons.title: The Three Jewels
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists take refuge in the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha.
reading: With the first followers, Buddhists say, the Three Jewels were complete. The first is the Buddha, the teacher. The second is the *Dharma*, his teaching. The third is the *Sangha*, the community.

Buddhists around the world recite words of "taking refuge" in these three. Refuge means a safe place. In Pali they say, "Buddham saranam gacchami," I go to the Buddha for refuge. Then they name the Dharma and the Sangha.
Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhists all honor the Three Jewels. The words and chants sound different in each land. The three jewels themselves are shared.

words.d: the Buddhist community, especially monks and nuns
a safe place to turn to

look.title: The Three Jewels
look.cite: The Three Refuges (Tisarana), Khuddakapatha 1, Pali Canon

check.q: What is the Sangha?
check.why: The Sangha is the community, especially monks and nuns.

check.q: What does refuge mean?
choices: a safe place to turn to
check.why: Refuge means a safe place.

check.q: What is the Pali form of Dharma?
check.why: Dharma is Sanskrit; Dhamma is Pali.

lessons.title: Great Students
lessons.mainIdea: The texts name Sariputta, Moggallana and Ananda among the Buddha's most honored students.
reading: The Sangha grew quickly, the texts say. Two friends, *Sariputta* and Moggallana, joined together. The suttas praise Sariputta for wisdom. They praise Moggallana for special powers of mind.

Ananda, the Buddha's cousin, became his helper for about 25 years. Upali, once a barber, became the expert on the rules. People from many backgrounds joined. The Buddha accepted people of any caste, the texts say.
In Buddhist temples today, statues of Sariputta and Moggallana often stand on either side of the Buddha. Buddhists honor them as model students. Visitors often see them there.

words.d: a leading student of the Buddha, praised for wisdom
a social rank a person was born into in ancient India

look.title: Two at His Sides
look.text: In many Theravada shrine rooms, a large Buddha image sits in the center. A smaller standing monk is on each side, hands pressed together. These are Sariputta and Moggallana.
look.prompt: Why might a temple place these two students beside the Buddha?

check.q: Which student is praised for wisdom?
check.why: The suttas praise Sariputta as foremost in wisdom.

check.q: What was Upali's job before he joined?
check.why: The texts say Upali had been a barber.

check.q: What is caste?
choices: a social rank you were born into
check.why: Caste was a birth rank in ancient Indian society.

lessons.title: The First Nuns
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya says Mahapajapati, the Buddha's foster mother, led women to become the first Buddhist nuns.
reading: *Mahapajapati* Gotami was Queen Maya's sister. She raised Siddhartha after his mother died. The Vinaya says she asked the Buddha to let women become nuns. At first he said no.
She and many women shaved their heads and put on robes anyway. They walked a long way to find him. Ananda spoke for them. The Vinaya says the Buddha then agreed, with eight extra rules for nuns.

Buddhists read this story in different ways today. Some see the extra rules as fitting their time. Others argue for equal treatment. In some Theravada lands, full ordination for nuns has been restored only recently, and debate continues.

words.d: the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, the first Buddhist nun
the ceremony that makes someone a monk or nun

look.title: Ananda Asks
look.text: Ananda asked the Buddha whether women who go forth could reach the fruits of the path. The Buddha said that they could. Ananda then asked him to let Mahapajapati go forth.
look.prompt: What question did Ananda ask first, and why does it matter?

check.q: Who led the first Buddhist nuns?
check.why: The Vinaya says Mahapajapati led the first women to ordination.

check.q: Who spoke to the Buddha for the women?
check.why: The Vinaya says Ananda spoke up for them.

check.q: Which book tells this story?
check.why: The story is in the Vinaya, Cullavagga 10.

lessons.title: Forty-Five Years on the Road
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says the Buddha walked and taught for about 45 years, staying in one place during the rains.
reading: Tradition says the Buddha taught for about 45 years. He walked from town to town in northern India. He spoke with kings, farmers, merchants and outcasts.

During the rainy season, he and the monks stayed in one place. Kind supporters gave them parks to live in. One famous park, Jetavana, was given by a merchant named Anathapindika. Many suttas were taught there.
He taught in ways that fit each listener. Sometimes he used stories. Sometimes he asked questions. The story of Kisa Gotami shows him teaching through something a person could do and see.

words.d: a park given to the Buddha by the merchant Anathapindika, where many suttas were taught
a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun

look.title: A Teacher Who Fits the Student
look.text: One teacher explains fractions with pizza slices. Another uses a number line. Both teach the same idea in a way their students can see. The suttas show the Buddha teaching this way too.
look.prompt: How did the Buddha fit his teaching to Kisa Gotami?

check.q: About how long did the Buddha teach, says tradition?
check.why: Tradition says about 45 years; he died at 80.

check.q: Who gave the Jetavana park?
check.why: The merchant Anathapindika gave Jetavana.

check.q: What is a lay follower?
choices: a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun
check.why: Lay followers are Buddhists living ordinary household lives.

lessons.title: Kisa Gotami's Lesson
lessons.mainIdea: In the mustard-seed story, Kisa Gotami learns that loss comes to every family.
reading: The story of *Kisa Gotami* is told in the commentaries on the Dhammapada and on the Therigatha. The Therigatha is a book of verses by early Buddhist nuns. Kisa Gotami's own verses are in it.
In the story, the Buddha does not scold her. He sends her on a search. Along the way, many families share their own losses. Buddhists say she learned that no one is alone in grief.
Teachers often tell this story when talking about loss. Buddhists see it as showing the Buddha's kindness. Hospice workers and grief groups sometimes share it too.

words.d: a grieving mother in Buddhist stories who became a nun
a Pali book of verses by early Buddhist nuns

look.title: Door to Door
look.text: Picture a road of small houses. At each door, a woman asks one question. At each door, someone answers with a name: a grandmother, a brother, a baby. The seed jar stays in her hand, empty.
look.prompt: What did Kisa Gotami learn at each door?

check.q: What did the Buddha ask Kisa Gotami to bring?
choices: a mustard seed from a house with no death
check.why: He asked for a mustard seed from a house where no one had died.

check.q: What is the Therigatha?
check.why: The Therigatha holds verses by early nuns, including Kisa Gotami.

check.q: What did Kisa Gotami do at the end of the story?
check.why: The texts say she became a nun.

lessons.title: The Buddha's Last Days
lessons.mainIdea: The Great Discourse on the Final Nirvana tells of the Buddha's death at Kushinagar at age 80.
reading: Digha Nikaya 16 tells of the Buddha's last journey. It is called the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Great Discourse on the Final *Nirvana*. The Buddha was 80 years old and ill.

He lay down between two sala trees near Kushinagar. He asked the monks if they had any last questions. None did. Then he gave his final words. Buddhists call his death the parinibbana, the final passing.
Statues of the reclining Buddha show this scene. He lies on his right side, calm, head resting on his hand. Buddhists in Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar have built very large reclining images.

words.d: in Buddhism, the end of suffering (Pali: nibbana)
the Buddha's final passing at death

look.title: The Last Words
look.text: Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!
look.cite: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: In your own words, what two ideas are in these last words?

check.q: Where did the Buddha die?
check.why: Digha Nikaya 16 places his death near Kushinagar.

check.q: How old was the Buddha when he died, says tradition?
check.why: Digha Nikaya 16 says he was 80. He left home at 29.

check.q: What is the Pali form of nirvana?
check.why: Nirvana is Sanskrit; nibbana is Pali.

lessons.title: Four Places of Pilgrimage
lessons.mainIdea: In Digha Nikaya 16, the Buddha names four places for followers to visit: his birth, awakening, first sermon and death.
reading: In Digha Nikaya 16, the Buddha names four places worth visiting. They are where he was born, where he awakened, where he first taught and where he died. These are Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar.
Buddhist *pilgrims* have visited these places for more than 2,000 years. King Ashoka set up pillars at some of them. Chinese pilgrims like Xuanzang wrote about them in the 600s CE.
Today Buddhists from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Japan, Tibet and America visit them. Many walk around the sites quietly, offer flowers and light lamps. Some come as families.

words.d: a journey to a holy place
the town where tradition says the Buddha died

look.title: The Four Places
look.prompt: Which place marks the first sermon?

check.q: Which place marks the Buddha's awakening?
check.why: Bodh Gaya is where Buddhists believe he awakened.

check.q: Which text names the four places?
check.why: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16, names them.

check.q: Which Chinese pilgrim wrote about these places in the 600s CE?
check.why: Xuanzang traveled to India and wrote about the sites.

choices: Setting the Wheel of the Dharma in Motion

Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha.

Every house she visited had lost someone.

review.q: In which position do reclining Buddha statues show him?
review.why: Reclining images show the Buddha on his right side at his final passing.

review.q: Which student is praised for special powers of mind?
review.why: The suttas praise Moggallana for powers of mind and Sariputta for wisdom.

review.q: Which is one of the four pilgrimage places?
review.why: The four places are Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar.
